Issued at 1221 AM CDT Thu Jul 23 2026

Current Conditions & Synoptic Overview:

At the surface, high pressure has built across the Midwest, with
ridging aloft across the western US and troughing along the East
Coast. The northeast quadrant of the ridge aloft is being 
suppressed by a shortwave trough ejecting across the High
Plains, and this shortwave is the forcing mechanism for a
cluster of showers across southwest Nebraska and northwest 
Kansas early this morning, as well as a narrow line of weak
radar echoes ahead of the shortwave across southeast Nebraska 
and into northwest Missouri. 


Rain Chances Today and Tonight:

As the high pressure slides east, surface and low-level winds
turn southeasterly across our area today. The shortwave is
progged to continue slowly moving across Kansas and Nebraska 
through the day today. A leading vort max ahead of the shortwave
moves across west-central Missouri this morning, bringing 
15-50% chances of showers with it as activity moves from Kansas 
into western Missouri. Coverage appears to become increasingly 
scattered with this activity as it progresses further east and
south, so many areas will likely stay dry, especially the
northeast portions of the forecast area.

850mb dew points increase gradually through the day, but 
sounding analysis indicates that much of the area will still 
have a fairly deep layer of dry air to overcome before precip 
reaches the ground. This decreases confidence that areas with 
showers visible on radar will see rain down at the surface this 
morning into this afternoon, with virga potentially dominating
for most of the day. There is little to no instability available
to help deepen the convection, so precip is expected to fall as
light showers today, with an isolated rumble of thunder possible
in the far southern portion of the CWA. HREF/REFS mean QPF
aligns with these expectations, with a very light QPF footprint
confined to areas generally along and west of I-49/I-29. 

Sounding profiles begin to moisten by this evening, when
isentropic ascent begins increasing and another leading vort max
pushes into the area ahead of the shortwave. Showery activity 
is expected to develop in northern Missouri along the narrow 
dCVA axis this evening due to the enhanced forcing, but the main
show for rainfall won't begin until late tonight into Friday 
morning.


Heavy Rainfall Potential Late Tonight Into Friday:

Lee cyclogenesis in the Plains intensifies tonight, lifting a 
warm front north along the 30kt nocturnal LLJ into southern
Missouri by Friday morning. Moisture advection intensifies with
the LLJ as well, exceeding 2.25" PW values by daybreak on
Friday. The main precip shield/MCS develops in eastern Kansas
after midnight, with most guidance suggesting the complex
reaches the western edge of the forecast area between 3AM-6AM
Friday. Initially, the complex should move more of a west-east 
direction as rain develops along the nose of the LLJ, but
movement is expected to pivot to move more northwest-southeast
through the morning and into the afternoon as the shortwave 
sags southeast through the day. The isentropic ascent is
strongest around and just after 12Z Friday, when convection is
expected to be strongest and most widespread. 

There are varying signals for how Friday may evolve. High-res
guidance suggests the system will generally be progressive, but
may see redevelopment behind the initial rain shield. 
Generally, rain will be primarily driven by isentropic ascent 
rather than pure convective processes, so stratiform rain
processes will likely dominate for much of the event.
Instability is meager (<500 J/kg), so there will likely be a 
few embedded rumbles of thunder and corridors of deeper towers 
with more efficient convective rain rates at times, but 
overall heavy rainfall and flooding threats are expected to
remain localized to the narrow corridors of deep convection
where rates can exceed 1.5-2" per hour. It may not be a complete
all-day washout in all areas, but most should expect rain 
through the morning hours and then at least on-and-off through
the afternoon and into the evening.

High-res ensembles also suggest that widespread accumulations 
will be measurable but not overly impressive or concerning, 
with most areas getting less than an inch of rain. However, HREF
and REFS LPMMs do show a few highly localized swaths of 
accumulations up to 5" where that deep convection occurs, which 
would be reasonable to expect within such a moist environment. 


Temperatures Climb This Weekend:

Rain and the associated cloud cover will help to limit 
temperatures today and tomorrow, so highs have been dropped a
few degrees accordingly, with highs in the upper 70s to low 80s.
The ridge aloft recovers from the shortwave intrusion and
